title: A spiral within a spiral
caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 498-G5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ESO 498-G5 · constellation Pyxis · about 100 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy ESO 498-G5, about 100 million light-years away in the constellation Pyxis, the Compass. Its arms keep coiling right into the middle, so the core looks rather like a miniature spiral galaxy of its own.

Many spirals instead have a bright, elliptical central bulge that appears as a glowing mass. Astronomers call those classical bulges, and call spiral-like centres such as this one disc-type bulges, or pseudobulges. Hubble, free from the blurring of Earth's atmosphere, helped show that both types exist, and that stars are still forming in disc-type bulges while classical bulges have stopped.

The two also differ in how their stars move. Stars in classical bulges swarm on random orbits, like those in giant ellipticals, while disc-type bulges echo the orderly arms. That suggests different origins: classical bulges are thought to grow through major events like mergers, and disc-type bulges slowly as stars and gas drift inward.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.05 x 1.59 arcminutes) and distance (100 million light years), the frame spans roughly 89,000 × 46,000 light-years. Its light set out about 100 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Galaxies can be a bit like Russian nesting dolls: a classical bulge resembles a small elliptical galaxy set inside a spiral, while a disc-type bulge looks like a second spiral at the heart of the first. The image combines visible and infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, covering about 3.3 by 1.6 arcminutes.
alt: A spiral galaxy whose arms wind all the way into its centre, making the core look like a small spiral.
